clue.text: A fruitful course, rejected, with reserve

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back the way it came, so this word is turned round

blocks.note: taken as written
a fool is a pudding of puréed fruit folded into cream, a course full of fruit

explanation.surface: A dessert full of fruit is sent back by a diner who is rather reserved.
explanation.walkthrough: A gooseberry fool is a classic British fruit pudding; read backwards it follows the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone aloof keeps their distance and stays cool and detached, which is behaving with reserve.

clue.text: Some shady development in official parking plans, maybe

definitions.text: Some shady development in official parking plans, maybe

blocks.clueFragment: Some shady development in official parking plans, maybe
blocks.note: surface reading: a dodgy scheme hidden in a council's car-parking proposals
setter's reading: a planting that gives shade, laid out in an official park of trees

explanation.surface: Something underhand has crept into the council's car-parking proposals.
explanation.walkthrough: Shady means giving shade, not crooked, and parking means laying out as a park, not leaving a car.
explanation.definitionFit: An arboretum is a botanical collection of trees planted and maintained for study, a park full of shade.

clue.text: Twisty sort of fellow took one in, then acted nobly

definitions.note: the answer is a person, one who acted and was a lord

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: Oliver Twist, the Dickens orphan, is a fellow surnamed Twist
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A devious man took somebody in, and then behaved with honour.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurence Olivier was the great stage and screen actor made a life peer, Lord Olivier, so he acted and was noble.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Olivier, the actor ennobled as a baron, literally performed on stage while holding a peerage.

clue.text: Just fine — but only just

blocks.note: first meaning: even-handed and right
a further meaning: dry and sunny, of weather
last meaning: middling, barely passable

explanation.walkthrough: There are really three meanings: just, fine and only just; the dash makes fine look like a comment on the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective covers impartial treatment, pleasant dry weather, and a mark that is merely adequate rather than good.

clue.text: Isn't in good form, apparently

blocks.note: surface reading: someone feeling off colour or playing badly
setter's reading: to look at, its shape is wrong, like a thing that fails to happen

explanation.surface: A player who is off their game, by the look of things.
explanation.walkthrough: Form means shape, not fitness; the word also splits as miss plus happen, which is what a thing that isn't does.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deformed has a twisted or badly made outline, so its physical form is far from good.

clue.text: Though sniffed at, used to bring the ladies round

definitions.text: Though sniffed at, used to bring the ladies round

blocks.note: surface reading: something scorned or looked down on

blocks.clueFragment: used to bring the ladies round
blocks.note: setter's reading: inhaled to revive fainting Victorian women

explanation.surface: Something despised that was nonetheless used to win women over.
explanation.walkthrough: Sniffed at means literally inhaled, and bring round means revive from a faint, not persuade.
explanation.definitionFit: These ammonia crystals were held under the nose of a person who had swooned to jolt them awake.

clue.text: Treated harshly by Fleet Street when in difficulties?

definitions.note: cryptic reading: handled hard by the press

blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: roughly treated by the newspapers
second meaning: under heavy strain, struggling

explanation.surface: Someone in trouble finds the newspapers kicking them while they are down.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street is the London street long home to the national newspapers, so it stands for the press.
explanation.definitionFit: Being under severe pressure and struggling to cope is the everyday idiom for being in trouble.

clue.text: See 6

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that the former Prime Minister is missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Heath looks like moorland; it is the politician, known to everyone as Ted.
explanation.definitionFit: To have noted something is to have seen it and taken it in, the same as having remarked or perceived it.

clue.text: It should move our people promptly, and what they do if it doesn't

definitions.text: It should move our people promptly

blocks.clueFragment: what they do if it doesn't

explanation.walkthrough: British Rail was the state railway of Great Britain until privatisation in the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: The nationalised railway existed to carry the people of the country on trains running to timetable.

clue.text: How he and she are loved, in love like this

blocks.clueFragment: How he and she are loved
blocks.note: surface reading: a couple deeply devoted to each other
setter's reading: the phrase for being utterly smitten

explanation.surface: A happy couple who adore one another.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase literally describes a tumble, but idiomatically it means completely besotted.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone so smitten that they are figuratively turned upside down by passion.

clue.text: Grave pledge?

explanation.walkthrough: Grave looks like a burial place; here it is the adjective. An earnest, as a noun, is money paid as security.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means sincere and solemn; the noun is an old term for a down payment securing a deal.

clue.text: See 9

explanation.definitionFit: Money that is mismanaged has been handled poorly, which is exactly the phrase for maltreated or misapplied.

clue.text: See 13

blocks.note: to entice is to lure
fortune is destiny

explanation.surface: Courting luck risks bringing down the goddess of retribution.
explanation.walkthrough: Nemesis is the Greek goddess who punishes arrogance, so provoking her means inviting disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to take a reckless risk that seems to invite misfortune, exactly what angering a vengeful goddess does.

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the pointed tip of an archer's shaft and a pond plant whose leaves share that shape.
